summary:
Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, and requiring medical certification for identity recognition. Human Rights Watch describes the amendment as reversing the self-identification principle set by the Supreme Court's 2014 National Legal Services Authority ruling.

Recognition now depends on documents an applicant must obtain or renew: medical boards and district authorities must certify gender-affirming surgery, and only people within the recognised categories can enter the scheme. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside it. The amendment also creates new offences, including up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender; Human Rights Watch warns the provision could criminalise support networks. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

India is estimated to have around two million transgender people. Of the 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, roughly 32,500 hold identity cards, so most people seeking recognition would be entering the certification process for the first time.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required by passport authorities to sit a medical examination. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units. Assessments of police conduct diverge: the United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited, non-systemic police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy.
tangentialFactors:
The government presents the 2026 amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking by targeting benefits at recognised groups. Critics, among them rights activist Akkai Padmashali, describe it as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, arguing that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. Human Rights Watch called the bill a huge setback and urged the president not to sign it.

The gap between population and documentation is large: an estimated two million transgender people against 487,803 census-recorded persons and about 32,500 identity cards issued. Any tightening of certification therefore falls on a population mostly undocumented.

Protection from sexual violence weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Bans on conversion therapy issued by the Madras High Court in 2021 and by the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating. Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Facilities and care access are set mainly at state level, so the package available varies sharply by where in India a person is located. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards, which is materially better than territories with none.
localsOnly:
Residents have access to state-level schemes that visitors do not. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras.

Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds was barred by the Allahabad High Court in 2021. The Madras High Court's 2021 S. Sushma judgment directed the National Medical Commission and education authorities on LGBTQIA+ protection, police sensitisation and conversion therapy.

Domestic recognition of relationships remains limited: there is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, though courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the March 2026 amendment was pending as of late March 2026. Whether it has since been signed, and on what terms, is unresolved in the sources available here.

No source in this inventory describes how the certification procedure is administered in Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu itself — which district authority receives applications, whether medical boards sit locally, or what processing times apply. Not sourced.

The effect of the 2026 amendment on identity documents already issued under the 2019 self-identification route is not addressed in these sources.

The incidents at Chennai airport and the Kolkata and Assam railway stations occurred in other states. Their frequency in Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu, and the conduct of the local police and territory administration, are not sourced.

Whether the territory operates a transgender welfare board or its own housing, pension or surgery schemes is not sourced. The extent of clandestine conversion-therapy networks is likewise undocumented.
